summary: The KJV has the speaker say “it was an error” before ‘the angel’. Brenton’s Greek has the same words said before the face of God.

title: “Nor known any thing” — the Greek has the unborn child not knowing “rest”
summary: The KJV says the untimely birth has not seen the sun nor known anything. Brenton’s Greek says he has not known rest.

Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/21/6/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ECC06.htm.
reasoning: The Hebrew clause printed is וְלֹא יָדָע, and the next Hebrew word is נַחַת, which the KJV places in the following clause (‘this hath more rest than the other’). The Greek takes that word as the thing not known: οὐκ ἔγνω ἀναπαύσεις, ‘nor known rest’. So the KJV says the child has no knowledge of anything, and the Greek says he has had no rest. The two sentences make different claims about what the child lacks.

title: “A thousand years twice told” — the Greek has no ‘twice’
summary: The KJV doubles the thousand years. Brenton’s Greek prints ‘a thousand years’ with a different second word and no doubling.

Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/21/6/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ECC06.htm.
reasoning: The Hebrew prints אֶלֶף שָׁנִים פַּעֲמַיִם, a thousand years, and then a word the KJV reads as ‘twice’. The Greek has χιλίων ἐτῶν καθόδους, which Brenton’s English gives as ‘to the return of a thousand years’. In the KJV the man lives two thousand years; in the Greek no figure above a thousand is printed. The sums differ by a factor of two, and the Greek second word is not a number.

title: “And in the sight of thine eyes” — the Greek adds “blameless” and a negative

Brenton’s own English (https://ebible.org/eng-Brenton/ECC11.htm) prints: “Rejoice, O young man, in thy youth; and let thy heart cheer thee in the days of thy youth, and walk in the ways of thy heart blameless, but not in the sight of thine eyes: yet know that for all these things God will bring thee into judgment.”.
